newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone junta says door still open for talks.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone junta says door still open for talks.

text.p: The military junta in Sierra Leone on Wednesday warned its West African neighbours against any military attempt to restore ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah and said the way was still open for peace talks.
"Our doors are still open for negotiations to solve the impasse," Abdul Sesay, the secretary general of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) told a news conference.
Talks between the junta and four neighbouring countries broke down last weekend when junta leader Johnny Paul Koroma said the army would be holding on to power until 2001.
The Nigerian-led ECOMOG military coalition said on Wednesday it would tighten a blockade of Sierra Leone to force the junta to relinquish power.
The force, whose main base is in neighbouring Liberia, warned ships and aircraft to keep clear of Sierra Leone territory.
"Any action in contravention of this warning is at the peril of the ship or aircraft," it said in a statement issued in the Liberian capital Monrovia.
The junta, which took power after a coup on May 25, responded with a warning to Nigeria that it would get bogged down in Sierra Leone if it started a military campaign.
"We are not capable of fighting the Nigerians but we are capable of resisting them," Sesay told the news conference.
"The Liberian case was meant to last six weeks but lasted seven years."

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) took that long to bring a civil war in Liberia to an end. The process was sealed with presidential elections last month that were won by the man who started the war, Charles Taylor.
Sesay said the ECOWAS ministers had failed to listen to the junta's case at the peace talks in Abidjan, Ivory Coast.

He said they had turned down a proposal to bring together coup leader Koroma, ousted president Kabbah and Foday Sankoh, the leader of the RUF rebels who had rallied to the coup. Sankoh is under house arrest in Nigeria.
However, Sesay added: "Any attempt now to bring back Tejan Kabbah as president will be met with very sharp difficulties as the RUF does not trust him."
The United Nations added to the pressure on the junta on Wednesday when the Security Council issued a statement threatening unspecified sanctions if civilian rule was not restored.
Council sources said the measures could include an arms embargo plus a travel ban on junta members and their allies.
The existing ECOWAS embargo has already caused severe shortages in the Sierra Leonean capital, Freetown, where most shops and banks remain closed.
There are few taxis on the road and most people are having to walk everywhere. Petrol on the black market is said to be three times the pre-coup cost.
Power cuts have become the norm, and oil industry sources said a weekend shipment of fuel oil from a ship that beat the sea blockade would not do much to improve the situation.
